concepts.def: Sustained rise in the general price level.
Sustained fall in the general price level.
Consumer Price Index — UK headline measure.

walkthroughs.body_html: The ONS picks a basket of ~700 items typical UK households buy. Each month they check prices nationwide. The CPI is the weighted average. Annual inflation = % change in CPI year-on-year. Bank of England target: 2% CPI inflation.
Demand-pull — AD rises faster than AS, 'too much money chasing too few goods'. Cost-push — input costs jump (oil 2022, wages). Both push CPI up. Often they overlap.

Winners: borrowers (real debt falls), workers with strong unions. Losers: savers (real returns drop), pensioners on fixed incomes, exporters if UK inflation higher than abroad. High inflation hurts confidence and investment.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.
A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
Demand always falls when supply increases.

mcqs.q: What causes the supply curve to shift?
options: Changes in production costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of producers, expectations — anything affecting supply other than the good's own price.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Inflation is when the economy grows too fast.
When demand rises, the supply curve shifts right to meet it.

sequence.def: Choose typical goods and services households buy
Record prices of basket items each month
Apply weights for how much is spent on each
Combine into a single price index number
Measure the index against a base year of 100
Percentage change in the index gives inflation
